response.title: For a months-long road trip sleeping in my pickup with a topper, what size power station and solar panel keep a fridge cold?
response.answer:
For a months-long road trip sleeping in a pickup with a camper topper, I'd recommend a 1,000–2,000 Wh LiFePO4 power station and 200–400 W of solar panels to keep a 12V compressor fridge running reliably.

My preferred setup would be 1,500 Wh of battery capacity + 300 W of solar + charging from your truck while driving. That gives you a good balance of reliability, portability, and cost.

The key is planning for cloudy days, hot weather, and times when you're parked in the shade—not just ideal sunny conditions.

1. How much power does a camping fridge use?

A typical 12V compressor fridge (such as a 35–55 liter Dometic, ICECO, or BougeRV) cycles on and off rather than running continuously.

These are planning estimates, not guaranteed specifications. The fridge's insulation, thermostat setting, ventilation, and ambient temperature all matter.

For planning, I'd budget 400–500 Wh per day for the fridge alone.

2. What size power station?

A 500 Wh station is too small for extended off-grid camping unless you recharge frequently. A 1,000 Wh station is workable, but 1,500–2,000 Wh provides a much more comfortable buffer.

3. How much solar do you need?

Solar panel wattage is the rated maximum output, not what you'll get all day.

Here are reasonable planning estimates assuming four equivalent peak-sun hours and 75% overall charging efficiency.

A 200 W panel could cover a fridge consuming 450 Wh/day in good sun, but cloudy days and shade can substantially reduce production. Dometic recommends at least a 100 W panel and a battery for its CFX3 fridge family; I'm suggesting more capacity because you're traveling for months.

A few things matter especially for a pickup topper:

Use the fridge's 12V DC cable, not the 120V AC inverter, to avoid unnecessary conversion losses.

Consider a DC-DC alternator charger if you drive regularly. Make sure it's compatible with the truck and power station; don't connect a large charging load directly to an unfused starter-battery circuit.

Keep the battery out of extreme heat. A sealed truck bed can get very hot in summer.

Ventilate the fridge's compressor area. Don't pack blankets or luggage tightly around its vents.

Keep the fridge at or below 40°F (4°C) and use a thermometer to verify food-safe temperatures.

Plan for shade. Roof-mounted panels are convenient while driving but produce much less power when you park under trees.

For a months-long road trip sleeping in a pickup with a camper topper, I'd recommend a **1,000–2,000 Wh LiFePO4 power station and 200–400 W of solar panels** to keep a 12V compressor fridge running reliably.

My preferred setup would be **1,500 Wh of battery capacity + 300 W of solar + charging from your truck while driving**. That gives you a good balance of reliability, portability, and cost.

The key is planning for cloudy days, hot weather, and times when you're parked in the shade—not just ideal sunny conditions.

## 1. How much power does a camping fridge use?

A typical 12V compressor fridge (such as a 35–55 liter Dometic, ICECO, or BougeRV) cycles on and off rather than running continuously.

| Conditions | Typical daily consumption |
|---|---:|
| Cool weather, efficient fridge | 200–300 Wh |
| Moderate weather | 300–450 Wh |
| Hot summer weather | 450–700 Wh |
| Very hot truck bed | 700+ Wh possible |

These are planning estimates, not guaranteed specifications. The fridge's insulation, thermostat setting, ventilation, and ambient temperature all matter.

For planning, I'd budget **400–500 Wh per day for the fridge alone**.

## 2. What size power station?

<box gap={2}>
  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **Battery capacity vs. fridge runtime**
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">At 450 Wh/day, no recharging</text>
  </row>
  {#each [{name:"500 Wh",v:500},{name:"1,000 Wh",v:1000},{name:"1,500 Wh",v:1500},{name:"2,000 Wh",v:2000}] as b}
    <box gap={1} key={b.name}>
      <row justify="between">
        <text weight="medium" size="sm">{b.name}</text>
        <text color="secondary" size="sm" tabularNums>{(b.v*0.85/450).toFixed(1)} days</text>
      </row>
      <box background="surface-tertiary" height="12px" radius="sm" clip>
        <box background={b.v===1500?"#16877B":"#8194A8"} width={`${b.v/2000*100}%`} height="100%" radius="sm"/>
      </box>
    </box>
  {/each}
  <caption>Estimated 85% usable energy, using the fridge's DC connection. Actual runtime varies.</caption>
</box>

A 500 Wh station is too small for extended off-grid camping unless you recharge frequently. A 1,000 Wh station is workable, but 1,500–2,000 Wh provides a much more comfortable buffer.

## 3. How much solar do you need?

Solar panel wattage is the rated maximum output, not what you'll get all day.

Here are reasonable planning estimates assuming four equivalent peak-sun hours and 75% overall charging efficiency.

| Solar array | Energy collected per sunny day | Assessment |
|---|---:|---|
| 100 W | 300 Wh | Marginal |
| 200 W | 600 Wh | Good for an efficient fridge |
| 300 W | 900 Wh | My preferred size |
| 400 W | 1,200 Wh | More margin for extra devices |

A 200 W panel could cover a fridge consuming 450 Wh/day in good sun, but cloudy days and shade can substantially reduce production. Dometic recommends at least a 100 W panel and a battery for its CFX3 fridge family; I'm suggesting more capacity because you're traveling for months. <Cite refs={["turn185443search0","turn185443search1"]}/>

      </box>

  <icon name="arrow-down" color="tertiary" size="lg"/>
  <box background="rgba(22,135,123,0.08)" border={{size:1,color:"rgba(22,135,123,0.35)"}} radius="md" padding={3} width="85%" align="center" gap={1}>
    <icon name="battery-charging" size="xl" color="success"/>

    <text size="xs" color="secondary">Compatible solar and vehicle inputs</text>
  </box>

  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="md" padding={3} width="85%" align="center" gap={1}>

- **Use the fridge's 12V DC cable**, not the 120V AC inverter, to avoid unnecessary conversion losses.

- **Plan for shade.** Roof-mounted panels are convenient while driving but produce much less power when you park under trees.

    </radio-group>
  </box>

    <grid-item>
      <label>Solar panel size</label>
      <select block value={solar} onChange={setSolar} options={[{label:"100 W",value:"100"},{label:"200 W",value:"200"},{label:"300 W",value:"300"},{label:"400 W",value:"400"}]}/>

This covers the modeled fridge use on days with the selected sunlight, but not extended cloudy periods.`:`Estimated solar deficit: ${Math.round(daily-harvest)} Wh/day. You'll need alternator charging, shore power, or more sunlight to sustain this indefinitely.`}</text>
  </row>
</box>

One question that would significantly change my recommendation:

**Are you planning to drive almost every day, or park in one camping spot for 3–7 days at a time?**

That determines whether you really need 300–400 W solar or could save money with a smaller array and more alternator charging.
